introParagraphs: Yardi Voyager is genuinely good at CAM reconciliation. That's worth saying upfront. If you run a large institutional portfolio and you've already invested in proper Voyager configuration, the platform handles gross-up, expense caps, and pro-rata allocation natively. There's a reason so much of the industry runs on it.

That said, "powerful when correctly configured" hides a real problem. Leases get amended. Staff turns over. Configuration drifts. And when it does, Voyager executes mathematically flawless but contractually wrong reconciliations, and the audit trail rarely makes it obvious why.

strengths.heading: What Yardi does well for CAM reconciliation
paragraphs: Yardi Voyager's CAM engine sits inside the Recovery and Reconciliation modules within Voyager Commercial. This isn't a bolt-on. The platform manages recoveries through relational tables tied directly to the lease record: expense pools, denominator tracking, and cap rules all live in the same database as your rent roll.

For teams that already run their whole operation in Yardi, this integration matters. When you amend a lease in Voyager, the system knows which recovery groups that tenant belongs to. When occupancy shifts, the denominator updates. You're not maintaining a separate spreadsheet and hoping it stays in sync with the GL.
The consultant ecosystem around Yardi's CAM module is also real: Assetsoft, Meissner CRES, and BC Solutions all specialize in configuring and managing Voyager reconciliation workflows.

callout.text: Yardi Breeze note: Breeze charges CAM as a flat-rate fixed dollar amount per rentable area. It doesn't support pro-rata allocation by tenant square footage, which makes it unsuitable for most multi-tenant commercial buildings.

painPoints.heading: Where Yardi CAM workflows create problems

items.title: Configuration drift
items.description: When a lease is amended (new cap, changed exclusion, renegotiated base year) someone has to update the corresponding fields in Voyager. If that doesn't happen, the system keeps calculating correctly against the old parameters. The output looks right. The numbers are wrong. This is the most documented failure mode on Yardi, and it's almost impossible to eliminate at scale.

items.title: Black-box calculations
items.description: Voyager's CAM engine runs stored procedures against a complex database schema. When the output looks wrong, tracing it back requires either database access or a consultant who knows where to look. Property accountants have posted about reconciliation errors where Yardi's own audit log showed conflicting math with no explanation.

items.title: Data portability
items.description: Getting raw CAM data out of Yardi for independent verification isn't straightforward. Standard financial reports export to Excel or CSV easily, but extracting the underlying recovery logic (denominators, expense pool assignments, cap calculations) requires either the proprietary ETL tool or custom SSRS queries that need database skills to write.

items.title: Cost and setup time
items.description: Mid-market portfolio pricing for Voyager runs $15,000-$100,000+ per year, on multi-year contracts with 90-day cancellation notice. Implementations take weeks to months and almost always require external consultants. You're not paying for CAM reconciliation; you're paying for a complete property management platform.

introParagraphs: Excel is free, familiar, and infinitely flexible. Most property controllers have been using it for CAM reconciliation for years. The process works. And industry sources commonly cite that material errors show up in roughly 40% of reconciliations.

The errors aren't from carelessness. They come from the nature of spreadsheet-based CAM: hundreds of manually-maintained formulas, cross-tab references that break when sheets are renamed, gross-up logic that made sense in 2019 but may not reflect BOMA 2024 standards, and cumulative cap banks that require year-over-year tracking across separate workbooks.

strengths.heading: What Excel does well
paragraphs: Excel is free, universally understood, and gives you complete control over your reconciliation model. For simple portfolios with a handful of tenants and straightforward NNN leases, a well-maintained spreadsheet can work reliably. The flexibility to handle truly custom lease structures is also a genuine advantage for edge cases.

painPoints.heading: Where Excel creates risk in CAM reconciliation

items.title: ~40% cited error rate
items.description: Industry sources commonly cite that roughly 40% of CAM reconciliations contain material errors. Most use spreadsheet-based processes.

items.title: No audit trail
items.description: Spreadsheets are easily overwritten. There is no stable record of what was calculated, when, and why. Tenant auditors exploit this - the burden of proof falls on you to reconstruct calculations from a workbook that may have changed since the statement went out.

items.title: Cumulative cap banking is manually fragile
items.description: Cumulative cap banking means tracking unused capacity across workbooks year after year. One broken cell reference and the entire history is wrong - with no way to know it happened.

items.title: Staff turnover risk
items.description: The institutional knowledge lives in the person who built the spreadsheet. When they leave, the new analyst inherits a model they didn't build and can't fully trust.

items.title: BOMA 2024 updates require manual maintenance
items.description: When BOMA updates its gross-up standards, someone has to update every formula in every workbook. Most don't.

The two tools serve opposite sides of the commercial lease relationship.

strengths.heading: What LeaseQuery / FinQuery does well (for tenants)
paragraphs: LeaseQuery's ASC 842 compliance capabilities are well-regarded in the mid-market. The platform automates right-of-use asset amortization, lease liability schedules, and journal entry generation - reducing the manual accounting burden for companies with significant lease portfolios.

LeaseQuery's integration with accounting systems (NetSuite, Sage Intacct, QuickBooks) ensures that lease accounting data flows into the broader financial reporting workflow without manual journal entry.

items.title: Designed for tenant-side lease accounting
items.description: LeaseQuery's core functionality - right-of-use asset calculation, lease liability amortization, ASC 842 journal entries - is built for corporate tenants recording lease obligations in financial statements. Landlords billing tenants for CAM expenses need the opposite: a tool that verifies outgoing bills are accurate, not one that records incoming lease costs.

items.title: No building-level GL ingestion
items.description: LeaseQuery does not ingest building operating expense data and allocate it to tenants. CAM reconciliation starts with the actual GL expenses - utilities, maintenance, management fees, insurance - not with the tenant's lease accounting. This data lives in the landlord's ERP, not in a tenant-side lease accounting platform.

items.title: No BOMA gross-up or cap enforcement
items.description: BOMA gross-up and expense cap enforcement are landlord-side calculations embedded in the lease terms. LeaseQuery helps tenants track what they owe; CapVeri helps landlords verify that what they're charging is correct under those same terms.

items.title: Tenant-side sophistication increases landlord risk
items.description: Tenants using platforms like LeaseQuery have better documentation of their payment history and lease terms than many landlords. If a tenant's automated platform flags a billing discrepancy, the landlord who cannot independently verify their own reconciliation is at a disadvantage.
